In [[algebra]], a '''seminormal ring''' is a [[commutative ring|commutative]] [[reduced ring]] in which, whenever ''x'', ''y'' satisfy <math>x^3 = y^2</math>, there is ''s'' with <math>s^2 = x</math> and <math>s^3 = y</math>. This definition was given by {{harvtxt|Swan|1980}} as a simplification of the original definition of {{harvtxt|Traverso|1970}}. 

A basic example is an [[integrally closed domain]], i.e., a normal ring. For an example which is not normal, one can consider the non-[[integral ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[x, y]/xy</math>, or the ring of a [[Node (singularity)|nodal]] curve.

In general, a [[reduced scheme]] <math>X</math> can be said to be '''seminormal''' if every [[morphism of schemes|morphism]] <math>Y \to X</math> which induces a [[homeomorphism]] of [[topological space]]s, and an isomorphism on all [[residue field]]s, is an isomorphism of schemes.

A [[semigroup]] is said to be '''seminormal''' if its semigroup algebra is seminormal.
